title: Jesus Washed Feet. Why Do Some Leaders Demand Thrones?
paragraphs: Jesus Washed Feet. Why Do Some Leaders Demand Thrones?

The night before the cross, the One who possessed all authority did something terrifying to human pride: He knelt. And if our Christianity keeps making us more entitled to honor instead of more willing to serve, we may need to ask whether we are actually becoming like the Christ whose name we carry.
There was a towel on His waist.
Water in a basin.
Dust on the feet in front of Him.
And within hours, nails would be driven through His flesh.
Do not rush past that scene.
Because the hands holding those dirty feet were the hands of the One through whom all things were made.
Jesus knew exactly who He was.
John makes that detail impossible to miss.
The Father had given all things into His hands. Jesus knew that He had come from God and was returning to God.
And what did the Son of God do with that knowledge?
He got down.
That may be one of the most devastating pictures of leadership in the entire Bible.
Because we often imagine that the more important someone becomes, the more people should serve them.
Jesus reveals something radically different.
The more clearly He knows His authority...
the lower He bends.
John describes the moment in the Greek text:
“ἤρξατο νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας τῶν μαθητῶν”
ērxato niptein tous podas tōn mathētōn
“He began to wash the feet of the disciples.”
John 13:5.
Not metaphorically.
Not from a platform.
Not through an assistant.
Jesus physically took their feet into His hands.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable detail is not merely that He washed feet.
It is whose feet were in that room.
Peter was there.
The man who would soon swear that he did not know Him.
The other disciples were there.
Men who would scatter when Jesus was arrested.
And Judas was there.
John explicitly places Judas's coming betrayal inside the setting of the meal before describing Jesus rising, taking the towel, and washing the disciples' feet.
Think about that.
Jesus knew betrayal was already moving toward Him...
and still reached for the basin.
Some of us struggle to speak kindly to someone who embarrassed us.
Some cannot forgive the family member who wounded us.
Some leaders become cold when their loyalty is questioned.

Some Christians can worship with raised hands on Sunday and spend Monday demanding recognition, defending status, collecting titles, protecting reputations, and punishing anyone who fails to honor them sufficiently.
Then Jesus kneels in front of people who are about to fail Him.
Suddenly our excuses become very small.
This article is not an attack on leadership.
Scripture recognizes leadership, elders, shepherds, teachers, authority, order, honor, responsibility, and accountability. Biblical humility does not mean pretending leadership does not exist.
The issue is not whether Christians should lead.
The issue is what Christian leadership is supposed to look like.
And Jesus did not leave that question unanswered.
After washing their feet, He said:
“ὑπόδειγμα γὰρ ἔδωκα ὑμῖν”
hypodeigma gar dedōka hymin
“For I have given you an example.”
John 13:15.
An example.
Not a publicity stunt.
Not a sentimental moment inserted into Holy Week.
An example.
Christ was showing His disciples the shape His authority must take in those who belong to Him.
And this is where the towel begins confronting the throne hidden inside us.
Because wanting a throne is not only a pastor's temptation.
It can happen to anyone.
You can demand a throne without ever standing behind a pulpit.
A father can demand one in his home.
A mother can demand one from her children.
A ministry volunteer can demand one through recognition.
A worship leader can demand one through applause.
A Christian creator can demand one through numbers.
A church member can demand one through influence.
A husband can call control “headship.”
A spiritual leader can call unquestioning loyalty “submission.”
A believer can call wounded pride “discernment.”
Sometimes the throne is not made of gold.
Sometimes it is simply the desperate need to be noticed.
To be thanked.
To be consulted.
To be praised.
To win every disagreement.
To have the final word.
To make people feel guilty when they leave.
To remind everyone how much we sacrificed.
To make ourselves indispensable.
And this is where Scripture stops being something we examine and becomes something that examines us.
Because before asking, “Why do some leaders demand thrones?”
perhaps we should whisper:
“Jesus... where am I demanding one?”
That question hurts differently.
James and John once came to Jesus wanting prominent seats in His glory.
They wanted proximity to the throne.
Jesus answered by redefining greatness itself.
In Mark 10, He contrasted the domination practiced by Gentile rulers with life among His disciples. The Greek becomes especially sharp:
“οὐχ οὕτως δέ ἐστιν ἐν ὑμῖν”
ouch houtōs de estin en hymin
“But it is not so among you.”
Then He says the one who wants to become great must become a διάκονος — diakonos, a servant, and whoever wants to be first must become πάντων δοῦλος — pantōn doulos, “slave of all.”
Then comes the reason:
Even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many. Mark 10:45.
There is the Christian revolution.
Jesus does not merely tell ambitious people to stop being great.
He tells them what greatness looks like in His kingdom.
Serve.
Give.
Lower yourself.
Spend yourself for others.
Not because you are worthless.
Because you belong to the King who did exactly that.
Christian humility is not insecurity.
Jesus was not washing feet because He had forgotten His identity.
John tells us the opposite.
He knew where He came from.
He knew where He was going.
He knew what the Father had placed into His hands.
And because His identity was secure, He did not need other people's submission to prove His significance.
That is worth reading twice.
When you know who you are before the Father, you do not have to turn everyone around you into evidence that you matter.
You can serve without being photographed.
You can apologize without losing your identity.
You can listen without surrendering truth.
You can celebrate another person's success without feeling diminished.
You can correct someone without humiliating them.
You can carry authority without becoming addicted to control.
You can hold a title without needing everyone to bow emotionally before it.
Jesus had nothing to prove.
So He could kneel.

And perhaps some of our obsession with thrones comes from the fact that somewhere beneath the religious vocabulary, we are terrified that if people stop applauding us, we will discover how insecure we really are.
So we collect recognition.
Followers.
Positions.
Honorifics.
Influence.
Access.
Platforms.
And none of those things are automatically sinful.
A platform can preach Christ.
Money can feed people.
Influence can defend the vulnerable.
Leadership can protect a congregation.
A large ministry can accomplish enormous good.
The problem begins when the platform stops being an altar and becomes a throne.
When ministry becomes identity.
When disagreement becomes disloyalty.
When accountability becomes “rebellion.”
When questions become threats.
When wounded people are treated as liabilities to the brand.
When the shepherd begins needing the sheep to feed his ego.
That is not the pattern Jesus gave us.
Jesus said:
“οὐκ ἔστιν δοῦλος μείζων τοῦ κυρίου αὐτοῦ”
ouk estin doulos meizōn tou kyriou autou
“A servant is not greater than his master.”
John 13:16.
So here is the uncomfortable question.
If our Master carried a towel...
why are His servants fighting over thrones?
But there is another danger here.
It would be easy to finish this article angry at pastors, bishops, ministry leaders, Christian celebrities, or someone who hurt you.
Please do not miss Jesus that way.
The Gospel is not primarily a weapon for exposing everyone else's pride.
It is first a mirror.
Maybe nobody knows about your throne.
Maybe yours sits inside your marriage.
Maybe you punish people with silence until they apologize.
Maybe you secretly resent people who receive the opportunities you wanted.
Maybe you serve faithfully but become bitter when nobody notices.
Maybe you post Scripture partly because you love Christ and partly because you desperately want people to admire your spirituality.
Maybe you give...
but need your name remembered.
Maybe you forgive...
but make sure the person never forgets what they did.
Maybe you call yourself a servant...
until someone actually treats you like one.
That last one exposes us.
It is easy to love the title “servant of God.”
It is much harder when serving costs something.
When nobody applauds.
When somebody misunderstands you.
When another person receives the credit.
When you wash feet and the feet walk away without saying thank you.
And suddenly we understand why we need more than leadership principles.
We need a Savior.
Because Christianity is not the story of morally superior people learning better management techniques.
It is the story of sinners who cannot cleanse themselves being rescued by the Son of God.
Peter initially resisted Jesus washing him.
“Lord, are You washing my feet?”
Then he protested.
Jesus answered with words far deeper than etiquette:
“If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me.”
Before Peter could imitate the washing...
Peter had to receive it.
Do you see the Gospel hiding in plain sight?
Before you become useful, you must admit that you need cleansing.
Before you serve Christ, Christ must save you.
Before your hands carry the towel, your heart must surrender to the One carrying it.
And the basin points forward.

John opens the scene by saying Jesus loved His own εἰς τέλος — eis telos: “to the end,” with the expression carrying the sense of His love reaching its full extent. The foot washing anticipates the sacrificial love soon to be displayed at the cross.
The towel was not the end of His descent.
There was a cross coming.
The One kneeling before dirty feet would soon be stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The hands washing dust away would be pierced.
The knees bending beside the basin would carry Him toward Calvary.
And Jesus would do something infinitely greater than wash dirt from skin.
He would give His life as a ransom for many.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Our scandal is deeper than corrupt leadership.
It is deeper than celebrity Christianity.
It is deeper than hypocritical ministers.
The scandal lives inside every human heart that wants God's throne while resisting God's rule.
We have all wanted to be our own king.
We have all sinned.
We have all needed cleansing we could never accomplish ourselves.
And Jesus came anyway.
He did not climb onto a human throne and demand that sinners crawl toward Him.
The King came down.
He served.
He suffered.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
And He rose.
That is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is coming down from a throne that was killing you and discovering that the rightful King is merciful.
Maybe you have been hurt by spiritual leadership.
Maybe someone used the name of Jesus while behaving nothing like Him.
Maybe Scripture was twisted to control you.
Maybe “honor” became a weapon.
Maybe your questions were treated as rebellion.
Maybe you were made to believe that protecting a leader's reputation mattered more than telling the truth.
Do not confuse someone's misuse of Christ's name with Christ Himself.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the towel.
Look at the basin.
Look at the cross.
Human leaders can fail you.
Jesus remains Lord.
And if you are a leader reading this, do not read these words merely thinking about someone worse than you.
Ask the dangerous prayer:
“Jesus, show me where I have loved the throne more than the towel.”
Show me where I demand what You never demanded.
Show me where my ego has disguised itself as authority.
Show me whether people around me are becoming more like Christ—or simply more afraid of disappointing me.
Show me whether I am building Your kingdom or quietly building a monument to myself.
And give me enough grace to repent when You answer.
That prayer can save a ministry from becoming a machine.
It can save a marriage.
A family.
A friendship.
Perhaps even a church.
Because repentance is not the death of Christian leadership.
Repentance is often where Christian leadership finally begins.
The greatest Leader who ever walked this earth knelt.
The highest King became the servant.
The sinless One died for sinners.
And the grave could not hold Him.
So no, the answer is not that Christians should despise leadership.
The answer is that Christian leadership must keep returning to Jesus.
Authority under His authority.
Strength shaped by His character.
Truth spoken with His love.
Courage without cruelty.
Conviction without vanity.
Leadership without idolatry.
A crown surrendered beneath the cross.
A towel within reach.
And perhaps tonight, the person who needs to surrender the throne is not “that pastor.”
Not that famous preacher.
Not your spouse.
Not your father.
Not your boss.
Maybe it is you.
Maybe it is me.
That is the uncomfortable beauty of grace.
Jesus does not expose our pride merely to shame us.
He calls us down because He loves us too much to leave us worshiping ourselves.

And if Christ has already been teaching you that leadership means serving rather than being worshiped, share part of your testimony. Someone reading the comments may need the hope God has already written into your story.
Then do something beyond commenting.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith—not a transaction we can buy.
But if this message is proclaiming truth that you believe another person needs, sharing it can become one small act of service.
Someone may be becoming the very kind of leader Jesus warned against.
Someone may be sitting quietly in a church wondering whether Jesus Himself is really like the people who wounded them.
Let them see the towel.
Send this to the Christian who is becoming influential before influence becomes their identity.
We need to return again and again to the Christ who kneels.
Jesus has already paid the price we never could.
Go back to the room.
Hear the water.
See the basin.
Watch the King kneel.
Then ask yourself whether the Christianity you are living looks anything like the Christ you claim to follow.
Because someday every earthly platform will disappear.
Every title will become irrelevant.
Every follower count will reach zero.
Every stage light will go dark.
Every human throne will become dust.
But Jesus Christ will still be King.
And astonishingly, the King who deserves every throne is the King who took the towel, went to the cross, conquered the grave, and still calls proud, broken, scandal-covered people into grace.
When everyone else is fighting for the highest seat, never forget the sound of your King pouring water into a basin.
